name: Mobwa Karen
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Shintani, Tadahiko 2017. The Blimaw language (ILCAA); Naw Veronica 2011 Payap thesis on Dermuha phonology; neither found online

new_statements.quote: In Dermuha, two types of word structures: single morpheme words and multiple morpheme words, can be found. The sesquisyllabic word structure that is found in many Southeast Asian languages like Mon-Khmer languages and Burmese language is not found in Dermuha. [...] In Dermuha, the word stress is not prominent, as it is hard to say whether stress is on the final syllable or the initial syllable. The longest single morpheme word found in this language has four syllables.
new_statements.citation: Naw Veronica. 2011. The phonology of Dermuha and a phonological and lexical comparison between Dermuha, Sgaw Karen and Pwo Karen. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai.
new_statements.locator: Chapter 3 Phonology of Dermuha, section 3.2 Word structure, p. 39 (PDF page 53 of 198)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dermuha (Mobwa Karen) is a tone language: every syllable is C1(C2)V plus one of four tones (high, mid, low, high-glottal), and there are no reduced/minor syllables. The author states that word stress is not prominent and that she cannot determine whether prominence falls on the initial or the final syllable, i.e. no stress rule is given; prominence, if any, is not phonologically salient.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The only related remark is that, unlike Sgaw and Pwo Karen, Dermuha has no sesquisyllabic (minor-syllable) words; polysyllabic words (up to four syllables in single morphemes) consist of full tone-bearing syllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, based on a 1,180-item elicited wordlist (citation forms) from three male speakers of the single Dermuha village Chaung-na-khwa (Si-Pin-Gyi), 17 miles east of Taungoo, recorded Jan-Feb 2009.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement is for Dermuha, the speech of one village (Chaung-na-khwa / Si-Pin-Gyi, eastern Taungoo district, c. 17 mi E of Taungoo on the Taungoo-Mawchi road), which the thesis places in the Bwe-Mopwa / Palaychi cluster (related dialects: Palaychi, Panapu, Palaychiderka, Sahter). Glottolog files the thesis under mobw1234 and ISO 639-3 lists Palaychi/Palakhi, Mopwa, Blimaw and Maleh as alternate names of Mobwa Karen [jkm], so Dermuha = a variety of mobw1234; but the thesis itself never uses the name 'Mobwa' and its own speakers say they descend from 'Mopwa', a Pwo-like group. Whether Shintani's 2017 'Blimaw' is the same variety is unverified (Bradley 1997 puts Blimaw under Central/Bwe-Western, Mopwa/Palaychi under Southern with Sgaw).

sources.locator: Chapter 3 Phonology of Dermuha, section 3.2 Word structure, p. 39 (PDF page 53 of 198)
sources.note: Sect. 3.2 Word structure, p. 39 (PDF p. 53): the sesquisyllabic/minor-syllable structure of Mon-Khmer and Burmese 'is not found in Dermuha'; 'In Dermuha, the word stress is not prominent, as it is hard to say whether stress is on the final syllable or the initial syllable.' Syllable = C1(C2)VT, every syllable carries one of four tones (high, mid, low, high-glottal; sect. 3.4, p. 58); longest monomorphemic words have four syllables. No secondary-stress remark.

sources.citation: Kato, Atsuhiko. 2021. Typological profile of Karenic languages. In Paul Sidwell & Mathias Jenny (eds.), The Languages and Linguistics of Mainland Southeast Asia, 337-367. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton (author preprint).
sources.note: Family-level only: sesquisyllabic words consist of 'the unstressed first syllable and the stressed second syllable' (Pwo/Sgaw examples, preprint p. 7); Mopwa is named among the Karenic groups and 'Palaychi is one of the languages of the Mopwa group (for more details on Mopwa, see Naw Veronica 2011)' (preprint p. 20). No Mobwa-specific stress statement.
